jiaozhi-province-ming.t: The twenty years of direct Ming Chinese rule over Vietnam after 1407, ended by Le Loi's ten-year war of resistance.
jiaozhi-province-ming.o: After defeating the Ho dynasty in 1407, the Yongle Emperor annexed the country as Jiaozhi Province, reviving an old Han name. The Ming administration was based at Dong Quan, present-day Hanoi, under military and civil commissioners.
jiaozhi-province-ming.r: Ming officials divided the province into prefectures and counties, imposed Chinese law, taxed salt, gold and forest products, and recruited labour and craftsmen for China. They removed books and historical records, promoted Chinese customs and schools, and conscripted local men. These policies provoked continuous rebellion, first under the Later Tran dynasty and then by Le Loi from Lam Son.
jiaozhi-province-ming.e: Le Loi's insurgency, begun in 1418, won major victories in 1426 and 1427, defeating Ming relief armies at Chi Lang. The Ming agreed to withdraw in 1427, and in 1428 Le Loi proclaimed the Later Le dynasty. Ming rule was the last period of direct Chinese rule in Vietnam.

jaisalmer-state.t: The Bhati Rajput desert kingdom of the Thar, whose golden sandstone fort and merchant mansions grew rich on the caravan trade between India and Central Asia.
jaisalmer-state.o: The Bhati Rajputs had ruled from earlier capitals such as Lodurva before Rawal Jaisal founded the fort and city of Jaisalmer on the Trikuta hill in 1156.
jaisalmer-state.r: Jaisalmer lay on caravan routes linking Sindh, Multan and Persia with Gujarat and the Ganges plain, and merchants paid for elaborate havelis such as the Patwon ki Haveli and for Jain temples inside the fort. The fort suffered sieges by the Delhi Sultanate in the 13th and 14th centuries. Later the Rawals accepted Mughal overlordship.
jaisalmer-state.e: Jaisalmer signed a treaty with the British in 1818. The decline of caravan trade and the rise of Bombay's sea trade impoverished it in the 19th century. It merged into Greater Rajasthan in 1949, and the fort, still lived in, is a World Heritage Site.

jumbe-state-of-nkhotakota.t: A Swahili trading state on the western shore of Lake Malawi, a hub of the slave trade and of Islam in the region.
jumbe-state-of-nkhotakota.o: Around 1845 Salim bin Abdallah, a Swahili-Arab trader from the coast connected with Zanzibar, settled at Nkhotakota on the western shore of Lake Malawi. Taking the title Jumbe, he made himself ruler over the local Chewa and built the town into a trading base.
jumbe-state-of-nkhotakota.r: Successive Jumbes ran a commercial state that shipped ivory and enslaved people by dhow across the lake towards Kilwa and the coast; David Livingstone, who visited in 1863, described the trade. Mosques and Koranic schools made Nkhotakota a centre of Islam among the Chewa.
jumbe-state-of-nkhotakota.e: The Jumbe signed a treaty with Britain in 1889 and cooperated with Harry Johnston for a time, but in 1894 the British deposed the last Jumbe and absorbed Nkhotakota into the British Central Africa Protectorate.

juliana-republic.t: A short-lived republic in Santa Catarina proclaimed by the Ragamuffin rebels in 1839, famed for the exploits of Giuseppe and Anita Garibaldi.
juliana-republic.o: During the Ragamuffin War, forces of the Riograndense Republic under Davi Canabarro and Giuseppe Garibaldi advanced north into Santa Catarina, seeking a seaport. Garibaldi's boats were hauled overland to the coast, and in July 1839 the rebels captured the port of Laguna, where the Juliana Republic was proclaimed, named after the month.
juliana-republic.r: The republic was confederated with the Riograndense Republic and governed by local supporters under the protection of the rebel army. It had little time to establish institutions. In Laguna, Garibaldi met Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro, known as Anita, who joined him in battle.
juliana-republic.e: Imperial forces counter-attacked by land and sea, and in November 1839 they recaptured Laguna after a naval battle in which Garibaldi's flotilla was destroyed. The rebels withdrew to Rio Grande do Sul, and the republic ended after about four months.

jashpur-state.t: A forested hill state on the borders of Chhattisgarh and Chota Nagpur, ruled by a Rajput family from Jashpur Nagar.
jashpur-state.o: Jashpur lay on the high plateau where Chhattisgarh meets Chota Nagpur. Its ruling family claimed Rajput origin and, according to tradition, displaced earlier tribal chiefs. The register dates the state to around 1600.
jashpur-state.r: The Raja ruled a population largely of Oraon, Kanwar and other Adivasi communities, with an economy of upland rice, forest produce and tea. It was one of the Chota Nagpur tributary states, transferred to the Central Provinces in 1905 and later to the Eastern States Agency. Christian missions became active among its Oraons.
jashpur-state.e: Jashpur merged into the Central Provinces and Berar in 1948 and is now Jashpur district of Chhattisgarh. Members of the former royal family, notably Dilip Singh Judeo, remained prominent in politics.

jaintia-kingdom.t: A kingdom of the Pnar people that ruled both the Jaintia Hills and the plains around Jaintiapur, known for its standing stones, annexed by the British in 1835.
jaintia-kingdom.o: The Jaintia kingdom grew from chiefdoms of the Pnar (Synteng) people of the eastern Meghalaya plateau, who extended their rule into the plains north of Sylhet. Its early history comes from oral tradition and later chronicles, and the register's start date is approximate.
jaintia-kingdom.r: The kings ruled the hills through local chiefs and the plains from Jaintiapur, combining Pnar custom with Hindu court ritual and worship of the goddess Durga. Monoliths at Nartiang and Jaintiapur mark royal and clan memorials. The kingdom fought and traded with the Ahom kingdom, the Kachari kingdom and the Koch rulers.
jaintia-kingdom.e: Accusing the court of seizing British subjects for human sacrifice, the British annexed the plains and then the hills in 1835, deposing Raja Rajendra Singh. A Jaintia rising against taxes followed in 1860–1862. The hills are now in Meghalaya; Jaintiapur is in Bangladesh.

justanid-dynasty.t: A Daylamite royal family in the valleys of the Alborz that sheltered Alid refugees and is credited with building the castle of Alamut.
justanid-dynasty.o: The Justanids were rulers of Daylam, the highlands south-west of the Caspian, with their centre in Rudbar on the Shahrud. They first appear in 791, when King Marzuban ibn Justan gave refuge to the Alid rebel Yahya ibn Abdallah, before handing him over to the Abbasid Caliphate.
justanid-dynasty.r: The Daylamites were tough highland infantry who long resisted Arab rule. The Justanids governed through clan loyalties and accepted Islam in the 9th century, often in its Zaydi Shia form under the influence of Alid missionaries. Justan III supported the Alavid dynasty of Tabaristan after 864, and tradition credits Wahsudan ibn Marzuban with building Alamut castle in about 860.
justanid-dynasty.e: From the early 10th century the Justanids were overshadowed by the Sallarid dynasty, who married into their family and took over Daylam. The family lingered as minor lords and disappears from the sources around the early 11th century.

jaunpur-sultanate.t: The Sharqi sultanate of the eastern Ganges plain, whose capital Jaunpur was a centre of learning and of a distinctive mosque architecture.
jaunpur-sultanate.o: In 1394 the Tughluq sultan appointed the eunuch Malik Sarwar governor of the eastern provinces with the title Malik al-Sharq, lord of the east. After Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 Malik Sarwar ruled independently from Jaunpur, founding the Sharqi dynasty, which was continued by his adopted son Mubarak Shah.
jaunpur-sultanate.r: Ibrahim Shah Sharqi made Jaunpur a refuge for scholars fleeing Delhi, earning it the name the Shiraz of India. The Atala Mosque and Jama Masjid of Jaunpur, with their massive gateway screens, are the finest examples of the Sharqi style. The sultans held Awadh and much of the Doab and frequently challenged the Delhi Sultanate.
jaunpur-sultanate.e: Husain Shah Sharqi's repeated attacks on Delhi failed, and Bahlul Lodi conquered Jaunpur in 1479. Husain Shah took refuge in Bengal, and Jaunpur became a province of the Lodi sultanate and later the Mughal Empire.

jafrabad-state.t: A small Kathiawar port held as a dependency by the Siddi Nawabs of Janjira, far down the western coast.
jafrabad-state.o: Jafrabad was a port on the southern coast of Kathiawar. In the later 17th century it passed to the Siddis of Janjira, the African-descended naval chiefs of the Konkan coast, who kept it as a distant dependency.
jafrabad-state.r: The Nawab of Janjira ruled Jafrabad through a local governor, and its income came from fishing, coastal trade and customs. The British treated it as part of the Janjira State, though it lay geographically in Kathiawar.
jafrabad-state.e: Together with Janjira, Jafrabad acceded to India and in 1948 merged into Bombay Province. It became part of Gujarat in 1960 and is a fishing port in Amreli district.

jhansi-state.t: The Maratha state of Jhansi in Bundelkhand, annexed under the doctrine of lapse and made famous by Rani Lakshmibai's resistance in 1857–58.
jhansi-state.o: Jhansi was taken by the Marathas from the Bundelas in the 18th century and held by governors appointed by the Peshwa, the Newalkar family. In 1804 the governor made a treaty with the British, and after the Peshwa's fall in 1817 the family became hereditary rulers of a protected state.
jhansi-state.r: The Newalkar Rajas governed Jhansi fort and its surrounding plain, a strategic point between the Gangetic plain and central India. Raja Gangadhar Rao adopted a son shortly before his death in 1853, but Lord Dalhousie refused to recognise the adoption.
jhansi-state.e: The British annexed Jhansi under the doctrine of lapse in 1854. In 1857 Rani Lakshmibai, Gangadhar Rao's widow, took control, and she fought the British until she was killed near Gwalior in June 1858. Jhansi was then absorbed into British territory.

jambi-sultanate.t: Pepper-exporting Malay sultanate on the Batang Hari river of Sumatra, whose last great sultan fought the Dutch for nearly half a century.
jambi-sultanate.o: Jambi stood on the site of ancient Malayu, but the Islamic sultanate took shape in the early 17th century. By 1615 Dutch and English traders had opened factories there to buy pepper grown in the upriver highlands, and the court used this wealth to rival Johor and Palembang for control of the trade of eastern Sumatra.
jambi-sultanate.r: The sultan presided over a riverine state in which downstream nobles controlled trade while upstream communities, including Minangkabau settlers, grew pepper. Jambi fought a long war against the Johor Sultanate and sacked its capital Batu Sawar in 1673. The decline of pepper prices after about 1680 weakened the court.
jambi-sultanate.e: The Dutch imposed treaties in the 19th century and deposed Sultan Thaha Saifuddin in 1858. He waged guerrilla resistance from the interior until he was killed in 1904, after which Jambi was annexed into the Dutch East Indies and later became a province of Indonesia.

jhabua-state.t: A Rathore Rajput state of western Malwa ruling over a largely Bhil population in the hills between Gujarat and the Narmada.
jhabua-state.o: Jhabua was founded around 1584 by Kesho Das, a Rathore Rajput, who received the title of Raja from the Mughal court after suppressing Bhil chiefs who had attacked imperial officials in the region. He took Jhabua from its earlier Bhil ruler and made it his capital.
jhabua-state.r: The Rajas governed hilly country of thin soils, where most of the population were Bhils and Bhilalas practising shifting and dry cultivation. In the 18th century the state paid tribute to the Holkars of Indore. Under British rule it was a salute state in the Bhopawar Agency of Central India.
jhabua-state.e: Jhabua acceded to India and in 1948 joined the union of Madhya Bharat, which became part of Madhya Pradesh in 1956. Its territory forms Jhabua district, still one of India's most tribal districts.

jushi.t: The oasis kingdom of the Turpan basin, fought over by the Han and the Xiongnu, whose dramatic cliff-top capital at Jiaohe still stands.
jushi.o: Jushi controlled the Turpan basin and the passes through the eastern Tianshan, the gateway between Mongolia and the Tarim. It was first a dependency of the Xiongnu. After repeated Han campaigns, often called the five battles for Jushi, it was divided around 60 BCE into Former Jushi, centred on Jiaohe, and Later Jushi north of the mountains.
jushi.r: Jiaohe was built on a narrow island plateau between two rivers, its buildings carved down into the loess. The people farmed irrigated fields and herded, and their kings shifted allegiance with every change in the balance of power. The Han stationed military colonists nearby under a Wuji colonel at Gaochang, which gradually became the region's main Chinese centre.
jushi.e: Jushi survived as a vassal of successive Chinese and steppe powers until around 450, when Juqu Anzhou, leader of the Northern Liang remnants who had seized Gaochang, destroyed it. The Gaochang Kingdom inherited the Turpan basin, and the ruins of Jiaohe are now a World Heritage Site.

joseon.t: Korea's last and longest-ruling dynasty, which made Neo-Confucianism the basis of state and society and created the Hangul alphabet.
joseon.o: General Yi Seong-gye seized power in Goryeo in 1388 after refusing to attack Ming China, carried out land reform, and in 1392 deposed the last Goryeo king to found Joseon. In 1394 he moved the capital to Hanyang, later Seoul, and Joseon accepted the Ming as overlord.
joseon.r: Kings governed with a Confucian bureaucracy drawn from the yangban class through civil examinations, guided by the Gyeongguk daejeon code. Buddhism lost state support. King Sejong promoted science and in 1443 created Hangul. Japanese invasions under Toyotomi Hideyoshi from 1592 to 1598 were resisted with the turtle ships of Yi Sun-sin and Ming help, but Manchu invasions in 1627 and 1636 forced submission to the Qing. Yeongjo and Jeongjo led an 18th-century revival.
joseon.e: Isolation ended with the Treaty of Ganghwa of 1876 with Japan. After the Donghak uprising and the Sino-Japanese War ended Chinese suzerainty, King Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897.

jobat-state.t: A small Rajput state in the Bhil country of western Madhya Pradesh, one of the minor states of the Bhopawar Agency.
jobat-state.o: Tradition dates the ruling family to the 15th century, but little is reliably known of its origins.
jobat-state.r: Jobat was a small, hilly state with a mainly Bhil population. It paid tribute to the Marathas and later came under the Bhopawar Agency of British central India. Its history is poorly recorded.
jobat-state.e: Jobat merged into Madhya Bharat in 1948, which became part of Madhya Pradesh in 1956. It is now in Alirajpur district.

jailolo-sultanate.t: One of the four kingdoms of the North Moluccas, on the island of Halmahera, absorbed by its rival Ternate in 1551.
jailolo-sultanate.o: Jailolo on the west coast of Halmahera was one of the four Moluccan kingdoms, with Ternate, Tidore and Bacan, known as the Moloku Kie Raha. Local tradition held it to be the oldest of the four. Its rulers accepted Islam in the late 15th century, as Muslim traders brought the clove trade under their influence.
jailolo-sultanate.r: Jailolo controlled parts of Halmahera, a source of sago and food for the clove-growing islands, and took part in the clove trade with Javanese and Malay merchants. Its sultans were often in conflict with Ternate and sometimes looked to Tidore and the Spanish for support.
jailolo-sultanate.e: Ternate, backed by the Portuguese, attacked Jailolo in the 1530s and 1550s, and in 1551 its sultan Katarabumi was forced to submit. Jailolo became part of the Ternate Sultanate. Its title was revived briefly in the 19th century by rebels against Dutch rule.
jailolo-sultanate.la: North Moluccan Malay, Galela and other North Halmahera languages

jamaican-maroons.t: Self-governing communities of escaped Africans in Jamaica's mountains who fought Britain to a standstill and won treaties of autonomy in 1739.
jamaican-maroons.o: When the English invaded Spanish Jamaica in 1655, many enslaved Africans fled into the interior and formed free communities. Their numbers grew as runaways from British plantations joined them, many of them Akan from the Gold Coast. Two main groups emerged: the Leeward Maroons of the Cockpit Country and the Windward Maroons of the Blue Mountains.
jamaican-maroons.r: Maroon towns were run by elected or chosen leaders, among them Cudjoe in the west and Nanny in the east, now a national heroine. They farmed hidden provision grounds, hunted wild hogs and used guerrilla tactics and abeng horn signals. After the First Maroon War, treaties of 1739 and 1740 granted them land and autonomy in return for returning runaways and helping suppress revolts, a clause that soured relations with the enslaved.
jamaican-maroons.e: In the Second Maroon War of 1795 to 1796 the Trelawny Town Maroons were deported to Nova Scotia and later Sierra Leone. Other communities, at Accompong, Moore Town, Charles Town and Scott's Hall, survive and still claim treaty rights, keeping Kromanti ritual language and traditions.

jigni-state.t: One of the smallest Bundela principalities of Bundelkhand, held by a junior branch of the family of Chhatrasal.
jigni-state.o: Jigni arose in the 18th century from the division of Bundela lands among the descendants of Maharaja Chhatrasal of Panna. It was confirmed to its chief by a British sanad in the early 19th century.
jigni-state.r: Only a few villages were attached to it, and little is recorded of its internal history. It was a non-salute state of the Bundelkhand Agency under a Rao.
jigni-state.e: After independence Jigni was merged with the other Bundelkhand states into Vindhya Pradesh, and its lands were absorbed into the Indian administrative system by 1950.

jin-korean-state.t: A shadowy early polity of southern Korea, named in Chinese records as the predecessor of the three Han confederacies of Mahan, Jinhan and Byeonhan.
jin-korean-state.o: Known only from brief Chinese mentions, Jin seems to have emerged in the southern half of the peninsula by about the 3rd century BCE, when it reportedly sought contact with Han China but was blocked by Gojoseon. Its people belonged to the bronze-using culture of slender Korean bronze daggers and mirrors.
jin-korean-state.r: Nothing certain is known of its government, which may have been a loose grouping of chiefdoms rather than a unified kingdom. Rich burials with bronze daggers, mirrors and bells suggest ritual leaders, and Chinese sources say that King Jun of Gojoseon fled south to this region around 194 BCE.
jin-korean-state.e: By the 1st century BCE the area had resolved into the Samhan confederacies of Mahan, Jinhan and Byeonhan, which Chinese texts describe as successors of Jin. Whether Jin was ever a single state remains debated.

judicate-of-cagliari.t: Southern Sardinian kingdom ruled by native judges from Santa Igia until Pisa destroyed it in 1258.
judicate-of-cagliari.o: The Judicate of Cagliari, also called Calari, took shape in southern Sardinia in the 10th and 11th centuries as Byzantine authority lapsed. Its capital was Santa Igia, near the lagoon west of modern Cagliari, and its judges came from the Lacon-Gunale family, who alternated the names Torchitorio and Salusio.
judicate-of-cagliari.r: Its judges ruled the largest of the four Sardinian realms, granting land and churches to Italian and French monasteries such as Montecassino and Saint-Victor of Marseille. Pisa and Genoa competed for influence; in 1216 the Pisans built the fortress of Castel di Castro on the hill of Cagliari with Judge Benedetta's reluctant consent.
judicate-of-cagliari.e: When the last judge, William III, allied with Genoa, the Pisans and their Sardinian allies destroyed Santa Igia in 1258. The judicate was divided among Pisa, Arborea, Gallura and the Pisan della Gherardesca family. Castel di Castro grew into the city of Cagliari.

jarwanid-dynasty.t: A Shi'a dynasty that ruled Qatif and the Bahrain islands in the 14th and early 15th centuries under the shadow of Hormuz.
jarwanid-dynasty.o: The Jarwanids took control of Qatif and the Bahrain islands in the early 14th century, displacing the Usfurid dynasty there. They are usually described as an Arab family of eastern Arabia and adherents of Twelver Shi'ism.
jarwanid-dynasty.r: The dynasty governed the coastal towns and pearl fisheries and depended on the Kingdom of Ormus, to which it paid tribute and whose kings sometimes intervened in its affairs. The traveller Ibn Battuta, visiting Qatif around 1331, described a town of Arab tribesmen who were committed Shi'a. Twelver scholarship flourished in Bahrain under their rule.
jarwanid-dynasty.e: Around 1440 the Jabrid dynasty, Sunni Bedouin from al-Ahsa, conquered Qatif and the islands, ending Jarwanid rule.

judicate-of-arborea.t: Longest-lived of Sardinia's four judicates, centred on Oristano, whose Eleanor of Arborea issued the Carta de Logu law code in Sardinian.
judicate-of-arborea.o: Arborea emerged in west-central Sardinia, around the Gulf of Oristano, as one of the four judicates that replaced Byzantine rule in the 10th and 11th centuries. Its capital moved from Tharros to Oristano around 1070.
judicate-of-arborea.r: Arborea was a kingdom in all but name, ruled by judges with a council of notables. Barisone II was crowned King of Sardinia by Frederick Barbarossa in 1164. In the 14th century Mariano IV fought the Aragonese conquest, and his daughter Eleanor issued the Carta de Logu in 1392, a law code in Sardinian that remained in force across the island until 1827. Its economy rested on grain, herding and salt.
judicate-of-arborea.e: Arborea's army was defeated by the Aragonese at Sanluri in 1409. In 1420 William III of Narbonne, the last claimant, sold his remaining rights to the Crown of Aragon for 100,000 gold florins, and Arborea became the Marquisate of Oristano.

jambughoda-state.t: A small forest state of eastern Gujarat, also called Narukot, whose woods are now a wildlife sanctuary.
jambughoda-state.o: Jambughoda, earlier known as Narukot, was held by a Rajput family in the forested hills near Champaner. The estate emerged around 1600, though its founding is known mainly from local tradition.
jambughoda-state.r: The ruler governed hilly country inhabited largely by Bhils and Naikdas. In the British period it was a minor state of the Rewa Kantha Agency. Few further details of its rulers are recorded.
jambughoda-state.e: Jambughoda was merged into Bombay Province in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960. Its forests now form the Jambughoda Wildlife Sanctuary in Panchmahal district.

jabrid-dynasty.t: A Bedouin dynasty that ruled eastern Arabia and the Bahrain islands in the 15th century until the Portuguese arrived.
jabrid-dynasty.o: The Jabrids, from the Banu Amir branch of the Banu Uqayl, were a nomadic clan of Najd. Around 1440 they took al-Ahsa and then Qatif and the Bahrain islands from the Jarwanid dynasty, establishing a Sunni dynasty based in al-Ahsa.
jabrid-dynasty.r: Ajwad ibn Zamil, the greatest ruler, made his state the strongest in eastern Arabia, extended influence to Oman and made the pilgrimage with a large retinue, receiving honours from the Mamluk Sultanate. The Jabrids followed the Maliki school, sponsored scholars and controlled pearl fisheries and caravan routes. Their relations with the Kingdom of Ormus moved between alliance and rivalry over Bahrain.
jabrid-dynasty.e: In 1521 a Portuguese and Hormuzi force took Bahrain; the Jabrid ruler Muqrin ibn Zamil was mortally wounded, beginning Portuguese Bahrain. The dynasty kept al-Ahsa a few more years before fading, after which the Ottoman Empire took the region.

jamtland.t: Self-governing farming province of central Scandinavia, ruled by its own assembly on Frösön until King Sverre brought it under Norway in 1178.
jamtland.o: Jämtland, around the great lake Storsjön in central Scandinavia, was settled by farmers who, according to tradition, governed themselves without a king. The sagas describe settlers from both Norway and Sweden, and the region lay between the two kingdoms.
jamtland.r: The Jamtamót, the province's assembly, met on the island of Frösön and decided law and justice. The Frösö runestone, the northernmost Viking Age runestone in Sweden, records that Östman Gudfastsson had Jämtland Christianised in the 11th century. The economy rested on farming, cattle, hunting and the fur and iron trade.
jamtland.e: In 1178 King Sverre of Norway defeated the Jämts and made them pay tax, and Jämtland became part of the Kingdom of Norway, though it belonged to the Swedish archdiocese of Uppsala. It passed to Sweden by the Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645, and the Jamtamót tradition is still a point of regional pride.

juthungi.t: A Germanic people north of the Danube in Bavaria and Franconia who raided Roman Italy in the 3rd century and were later absorbed into the Alemanni.
juthungi.o: The Juthungi were probably a branch of the Semnones who settled north of the upper Danube after the fall of the Raetian Limes. They first appear around 260; an altar found at Augsburg in 1992 records a Roman victory over 'Semnones or Iouthungi' who were returning from Italy with thousands of captives.
juthungi.r: Their society was led by warrior elites capable of mounting long-range raids. In 270 they invaded Italy, and the historian Dexippus preserves a speech of their envoys to Emperor Aurelian claiming 40,000 horsemen. Aurelian defeated them, and Rome later recruited Juthungi as soldiers.
juthungi.e: Juthungi raided Raetia again in the 350s and 383, and Aetius fought them in 429 to 430, their last mention. They are generally thought to have merged with the Alemanni, whose Bavarian and Franconian neighbours inherited their land.

junagadh-state.t: The Babi Nawabs' state in southern Saurashtra, home of Girnar and Somnath, whose ruler's accession to Pakistan in 1947 sparked a famous crisis.
junagadh-state.o: Muhammad Sher Khan Babi, a Pathan officer of the Mughal administration in Gujarat, declared himself independent at Junagadh in 1748, taking the name Bahadur Khanji. His family had served in Gujarat since the 17th century.
junagadh-state.r: The Nawabs governed a mostly Hindu population that included the sacred Girnar hill and the temple of Somnath. They accepted British supremacy in 1807 and ranked as a salute state of the Kathiawar Agency. Mahabat Khanji III, known for his many dogs, protected the last Asiatic lions in the Gir forest, then a royal hunting reserve.
junagadh-state.e: Advised by his diwan Shah Nawaz Bhutto, Mahabat Khanji acceded to Pakistan in 1947. Indian blockade and a provisional government in exile led him to flee, and India took over in November. A plebiscite in February 1948 voted overwhelmingly for India, and Junagadh joined the United State of Saurashtra.

jodhpur-state.t: Marwar, the largest Rajput kingdom of the Thar, ruled by the Rathores from the fortress of Mehrangarh, whose warriors served and fought the Mughal emperors.
jodhpur-state.o: The Rathores trace their rule to Rao Siha, who settled near Pali in the 13th century. Rao Chunda took Mandore around 1395, and in 1459 Rao Jodha founded Jodhpur and the hilltop fort of Mehrangarh as a new capital.
jodhpur-state.r: Rao Maldeo (r. 1532–1562) made Marwar a regional power before Sher Shah's Sur Empire defeated his army at Sammel in 1544. Later Rathore princes became Mughal commanders, but when Aurangzeb tried to take Marwar after Jaswant Singh's death in 1678, Durgadas Rathore led a long resistance. Marwari merchants spread across India as traders and bankers.
jodhpur-state.e: Jodhpur signed a treaty with the British in 1818. In 1947 Maharaja Hanwant Singh briefly considered joining Pakistan before acceding to India, and in 1949 Jodhpur merged into Greater Rajasthan.

jamkhandi-state.t: A Patwardhan Brahmin state in the southern Maratha country, formed when the Patwardhan family divided its lands in 1811.
jamkhandi-state.o: The Patwardhans, Chitpavan Brahmin commanders of the Peshwas, held extensive jagirs between the Krishna and the Tungabhadra. In 1811 these were divided among branches of the family, and Jamkhandi became a separate state under Gopalrao Patwardhan.
jamkhandi-state.r: Jamkhandi was a state of the Southern Maratha Country, later the Deccan States Agency, with a Marathi-speaking ruling house over a largely Kannada-speaking population. Its rulers built schools and in the 20th century moved towards representative government.
jamkhandi-state.e: After accession to India Jamkhandi was merged into Bombay State in 1948, and since 1956 it has been part of Karnataka, in Bagalkot district.

janjira-state.t: An island fortress state on the Konkan coast ruled by Siddis of African descent, whose sea fort at Murud resisted both Shivaji and the Portuguese.
janjira-state.o: The Siddis, Muslims of East African (Habshi) origin, held the island fort of Janjira off Murud as officers of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate; tradition dates their control to 1489. They later served the Bijapur Sultanate and then acted as admirals of the Mughal fleet on the west coast.
janjira-state.r: From the island fortress the Siddi Nawabs commanded the coast south of Bombay and its sea trade. Shivaji and his son Sambhaji both failed to take Janjira, despite building the rival fort of Padmadurg nearby. The state also held Jafrabad in Kathiawar. Succession passed among the Siddi families rather than strictly from father to son.
janjira-state.e: Janjira came under British protection in the 19th century and merged into Bombay State in 1948. The fort, never taken by storm, stands in Raigad district, Maharashtra.

jhalawar-state.t: A Rajput state carved out of Kota in 1838 for the heirs of the regent Zalim Singh Jhala, ruled from Jhalrapatan.
jhalawar-state.o: Zalim Singh Jhala was the powerful regent of Kota in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, and his descendants held the real power there. To end the rivalry between them and the Kota ruler, the British in 1838 created a separate state from part of Kota for his grandson Madan Singh.
jhalawar-state.r: Jhalawar was a 13-gun salute state of the Rajputana Agency, ruled by a Jhala Rajput Maharaj Rana. Its capital lay beside the old temple town of Jhalrapatan. Bhawani Singh (ruled 1899–1929) was known for his learning and interest in education, and later rulers continued to build schools and libraries.
jhalawar-state.e: Jhalawar acceded to India and in 1948 was merged into the United State of Rajasthan; it is now a district of Rajasthan.

jinhan.t: A confederacy of twelve statelets in southeastern Korea, one of which, Saro, grew into the kingdom of Silla.
jinhan.o: Jinhan formed in the 1st century BCE in the Gyeongju and Daegu area east of the Nakdong river. Chinese records claim its founders were refugees fleeing forced labour under the Qin dynasty, which may reflect migration from the north after the fall of Gojoseon.
jinhan.r: Twelve statelets, each with chiefs of graded rank, farmed rice, raised silkworms and rode horses and oxen. They produced iron like their Byeonhan neighbours and traded it widely. Early on they are said to have acknowledged the Jin king of Mahan as overlord, and their customs and language were close to Byeonhan's.
jinhan.e: The statelet of Saro, centred on Gyeongju, gradually absorbed its neighbours during the 3rd and 4th centuries and became the kingdom of Silla, completing the takeover by about 300.

jawhar-state.t: A Koli princely state in the Sahyadri foothills north-east of Mumbai, ruled by the Mukne dynasty until independence.
jawhar-state.o: The Mukne family, of the Koli community, established a chiefship in the hills of the northern Konkan; tradition dates the state to 1343. Its early history rests largely on family tradition.
jawhar-state.r: Jawhar was a hilly, forested state with a large Warli and Koli population. It came under the Marathas in the 18th century and under British protection in the 19th, as one of the smaller states of the Bombay Presidency. The Jai Vilas palace at Jawhar was built by its later rulers.
jawhar-state.e: Jawhar merged into Bombay State after Indian independence and is now in Palghar district, Maharashtra.

jaora-state.t: A Pathan Nawabi state in Malwa founded by a lieutenant of the freebooter Amir Khan, known for the Muharram shrine of Hussain Tekri.
jaora-state.o: Abdul Ghafur Khan, a Pathan cavalry commander and brother-in-law of Amir Khan, the founder of Tonk State, received Jaora and nearby lands from the Holkars of Indore State around 1808. The British confirmed his possession by the Treaty of Mandsaur in 1818.
jaora-state.r: Jaora was a 13-gun salute state of the Malwa Agency, with a Muslim ruling house over a mainly Hindu population growing opium and cotton. The Nawabs held Piploda State as a tributary. The shrine of Hussain Tekri, built by a Nawab in the 19th century, draws pilgrims during Muharram.
jaora-state.e: After accession to India Jaora was merged into Madhya Bharat in 1948 and joined Madhya Pradesh in 1956; it is in Ratlam district.

japanese-occupation-of-malaya.t: Japanese wartime rule of Malaya and Singapore, renamed Syonan, which shattered British prestige and hardened communal divisions.
japanese-occupation-of-malaya.o: Japanese troops landed at Kota Bharu on 8 December 1941 and advanced rapidly down the peninsula under General Tomoyuki Yamashita. Singapore surrendered on 15 February 1942, the largest capitulation in British history. The territories of the Straits Settlements, Federated Malay States and Unfederated Malay States were placed under Japanese military administration, with Singapore renamed Syonan-to.
japanese-occupation-of-malaya.r: Chinese residents, seen as hostile, were targeted in the Sook Ching massacres of 1942, which killed tens of thousands. Malays were courted while Indians were recruited into the Indian National Army. Food shortages, inflation and forced labour, including on the Burma Railway, were severe. In 1943 Japan handed four northern Malay states to Thailand. The communist-led MPAJA waged guerrilla resistance.
japanese-occupation-of-malaya.e: Japan surrendered in August 1945, and British forces returned in September under a British Military Administration. The occupation weakened colonial authority and strengthened both Malay nationalism and the communists, leading to the Malayan Union and the Malayan Emergency.
japanese-occupation-of-malaya.re: Sunni Islam, Buddhism, Chinese folk religion, Hinduism

janggala.t: The eastern of the two kingdoms created when Airlangga divided East Java in 1045, remembered in the Panji romances.
janggala.o: Janggala arose around 1045 from Airlangga's partition of Kahuripan, which gave one son the eastern lands around the Brantas delta, the old capital Kahuripan and the coastal ports near modern Surabaya and Sidoarjo. The other son received the Kediri Kingdom, also called Panjalu.
janggala.r: Very few records survive. An inscription of 1052 names King Mapanji Garasakan, who seems to have fought his western rival. Its coastal position gave it access to sea trade, but documentary evidence for its government is slight.
janggala.e: Janggala was absorbed by Kediri by the early 12th century; an inscription of King Jayabaya of 1135 declares 'Panjalu jayati', Panjalu is victorious. Its memory lived on in the Panji tales, in which a prince of Janggala searches for his beloved princess of Kediri, stories that spread across Southeast Asia.

jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state.t: The Dogra kingdom created by the Treaty of Amritsar in 1846, whose disputed accession in 1947 began the Kashmir conflict.
jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state.o: Gulab Singh, a Dogra noble who had served Ranjit Singh and became Raja of Jammu, extended his rule to Ladakh. After the First Anglo-Sikh War, the British sold him the Kashmir valley by the Treaty of Amritsar in 1846, creating a large state under the Dogra dynasty.
jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state.r: The Dogra Maharajas, Hindu rulers of a Muslim-majority population, governed Jammu, Kashmir, Ladakh and later Gilgit. Ranbir Singh codified laws; Pratap Singh accepted British supervision. Heavy taxes and discrimination against Muslims provoked the 1931 agitation that brought Sheikh Abdullah to prominence. Kashmiri shawls, saffron and timber were key products.
jammu-and-kashmir-princely-state.e: Hari Singh delayed choosing between India and Pakistan in 1947. After a Pashtun tribal invasion he acceded to India in October 1947, triggering war and a ceasefire in 1949 that divided the state. The monarchy was abolished in 1952.

japanese-occupation-of-british-borneo.t: Japanese military rule of Sarawak, Brunei, Labuan and North Borneo during the Second World War, ending in the Sandakan death marches.
japanese-occupation-of-british-borneo.o: Japanese forces landed at Miri in Sarawak on 16 December 1941, seeking its oilfields, and took Kuching on 24 December. Brunei, Labuan and North Borneo fell by January 1942. The former Raj of Sarawak, Brunei and North Borneo were united as Kita Boruneo under the Imperial Japanese Army, with headquarters at Kuching.
japanese-occupation-of-british-borneo.r: The occupiers ran the oilfields and requisitioned food and labour, causing shortages. Chinese communities suffered reprisals, and the Jesselton revolt led by Albert Kwok in October 1943 was crushed with mass executions. Prisoners of war and civilians were held at camps such as Batu Lintang near Kuching.
japanese-occupation-of-british-borneo.e: In 1945 Allied prisoners at Sandakan were forced on death marches to Ranau, and only six of some 2,400 survived. Australian forces landed at Tarakan, Labuan and Brunei Bay from May to July 1945, and the Japanese surrendered in September. Britain then created the Crown Colony of Sarawak and the Crown Colony of North Borneo.

jirang-state.t: A small Khasi chiefdom on the northern slopes of the Meghalaya plateau, one of the 25 Khasi states that acceded to India in 1948.
jirang-state.o: Hima Jirang was one of the Khasi chiefdoms of the Meghalaya plateau, lying towards the Assam plains in the present Ri Bhoi area. Its origins are known only from oral tradition, and the register's start date is approximate.
jirang-state.r: Jirang was headed by a Syiem chosen from a royal clan, with succession through the female line and decisions taken with clan elders. Little written record of its history exists.
jirang-state.e: Jirang came under British supervision in the 19th century and acceded to India in 1948, joining Assam. It is now part of Meghalaya.

jatprole-samasthan.t: The largest of the Telugu samasthans under the Nizams of Hyderabad, ruled by the Velama family of Surabhi from Kollapur.
jatprole-samasthan.o: Jatprole was a hereditary estate held by the Surabhi family, Velama chiefs who had served earlier Telugu and Deccan rulers. By about 1600 they held lands in the Krishna valley, in what is now Nagarkurnool district, and kept them under the Qutb Shahis and the Nizams.
jatprole-samasthan.r: As a samasthan, Jatprole was a tributary estate within Hyderabad State rather than a separate treaty state, paying peshkash to the Nizam while governing internally through its Raja. Its rulers patronised Telugu literature and temples, and moved their seat to Kollapur.
jatprole-samasthan.e: With the annexation of Hyderabad by India in 1948 and the abolition of jagirs and samasthans soon after, Jatprole ceased to exist. Its lands lie in Telangana.

jetpur-state.t: A Kathi state of central Saurashtra, held by branches of the Vala Kathi clan that also ruled Bilkha.
jetpur-state.o: Jetpur came under the Vala branch of the Kathis, a pastoral warrior community that gave its name to Kathiawar, around 1760. The holding was divided among several shareholders of the same family.
jetpur-state.r: The Kathi Darbars governed Jetpur and its villages under the Kathiawar Agency, with land shared between branches in a way typical of Kathi tenure. The state was minor, and little detail of its administration is recorded.
jetpur-state.e: After accession to India Jetpur was merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948. The town, now in Rajkot district of Gujarat, is known for textile dyeing and printing.

judicate-of-gallura.t: One of the four medieval kingdoms of Sardinia, in the island's north-east, ruled by native judges and later by the Visconti of Pisa.
judicate-of-gallura.o: As Byzantine control of Sardinia faded in the 9th and 10th centuries, the island divided into four self-governing realms, each ruled by a judge (iudex), who acted as a king. Gallura, in the north-east, emerged by the 11th century with its capital at Civita, near modern Olbia.
judicate-of-gallura.r: The judges ruled with an assembly of notables (corona de logu), drawing income from royal estates, herding and coastal trade. In the 12th and 13th centuries Gallura fell under the influence of Pisa, and through marriage it passed to the Pisan Visconti family. The last judge, Nino Visconti, appears as a friend of Dante in the Purgatorio.
judicate-of-gallura.e: Nino Visconti was expelled from Pisa in 1288, and the Pisan commune took over Gallura directly. The territory later passed to the Crown of Aragon after its conquest of Sardinia in the 14th century.

july-monarchy.t: The liberal 'bourgeois monarchy' of Louis-Philippe, King of the French, which rose from the barricades of 1830 and fell to those of 1848.
july-monarchy.o: The July Revolution of 1830 drove out Charles X of the Bourbon Restoration. Liberal deputies offered the throne to his cousin Louis-Philippe, Duke of Orléans, who took the title King of the French and accepted a revised Charter that lowered property qualifications and limited royal power.
july-monarchy.r: Government rested on a narrow electorate of wealthy men, and ministers such as François Guizot and Adolphe Thiers alternated in power. Railways, banking and industry grew, and the conquest of Algeria continued. The regime crushed republican and workers' risings, including the Lyon silk workers' revolts of 1831 and 1834. Guizot resisted all demands to widen the vote.
july-monarchy.e: An economic crisis and a banned campaign of political banquets led to revolution in Paris in February 1848. Louis-Philippe abdicated and fled to England, and the French Second Republic was proclaimed.

jaswan-state.t: A Katoch Rajput hill state in the Jaswan Dun, an offshoot of Kangra whose Raja lost his lands after joining the revolt of 1848.
jaswan-state.o: Jaswan was founded as a branch of the Katoch dynasty of Kangra State; tradition places the split around 1170. Its capital was Rajpura in the Jaswan Dun, the valley of the Sohan near modern Una.
jaswan-state.r: A small agricultural state, Jaswan was often dominated by Kangra and later by the Sikh Empire. Ranjit Singh annexed it in 1815, leaving the Raja a jagir.
jaswan-state.e: The British confirmed the jagir in 1846, but Raja Umed Singh joined the rising of the hill chiefs during the Second Anglo-Sikh War in 1848, and his lands were confiscated in 1849. The area is now in Una district, Himachal Pradesh.

jin-dynasty-1115-1234.t: The empire of the Jurchen people, who overthrew the Khitan Liao, drove the Song from northern China and ruled it until the Mongol conquest.
jin-dynasty-1115-1234.o: Wanyan Aguda, chief of the Jurchen tribes of Manchuria, rebelled against the Liao dynasty in 1114 and proclaimed himself emperor of Great Jin ('Gold') in 1115, ruling from Huining. Allied with the Song Dynasty, the Jurchen destroyed Liao by 1125, then turned on Song, sacking Kaifeng in 1127 and carrying off two Song emperors.
jin-dynasty-1115-1234.r: The Jurchen kept their own military organisation, the meng'an mouke units, settling soldiers among Chinese farmers, while governing through Chinese-style ministries and examinations. A Jurchen script was created. Prince Hailing moved the capital to Zhongdu (Beijing) in 1153, and under Emperor Shizong the dynasty promoted Jurchen traditions while Confucian culture flourished. The 1141 treaty fixed the Song border on the Huai river.
jin-dynasty-1115-1234.e: Genghis Khan invaded in 1211; Zhongdu fell in 1215 and the court moved to Kaifeng. In 1234 Mongol and Southern Song armies took Caizhou, and the emperor Aizong killed himself. The Jurchen later re-emerged as the Manchus of the Later Jin (1616-1636).

jasdan-state.t: The leading Kathi state of central Kathiawar, ruled by a Khachar Kathi Darbar from Jasdan.
jasdan-state.o: Jasdan was held by the Khachar clan of Kathis, a pastoral warrior people who gave Kathiawar its name. The Khachars established their rule at Jasdan around 1665 and expanded it through the 18th century.
jasdan-state.r: The Darbar ruled cotton and grazing country, paying tribute to the Gaekwads and Junagadh before British protection after 1807. It was among the larger Kathi holdings, though few details of individual rulers are widely recorded.
jasdan-state.e: Jasdan merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960. It is now a town in Rajkot district.

jarrahids.t: Bedouin emirs of the Tayy tribe who dominated Palestine around Ramla and for a time challenged Fatimid rule by backing a rival caliph.
jarrahids.o: The Banu Jarrah, a leading clan of the Tayy, entered Palestine in the later 10th century as the Fatimids struggled to control Syria. Their chief Mufarrij ibn Daghfal alternated between serving and fighting the Fatimids and by the 980s held much of the country around Ramla.
jarrahids.r: The Jarrahids ruled as tribal emirs, collecting revenues and protection payments rather than building a state administration. In 1011-1013 Mufarrij proclaimed the sharif of Mecca, Abu'l-Futuh, as an anti-caliph in Ramla before making peace with Cairo. His son Hassan joined the Mirdasids and the Kalb in a 1024 alliance to partition Syria, but the Fatimids defeated it at al-Uqhuwana in 1029.
jarrahids.e: Driven from Palestine, Hassan and his followers took service with Byzantium. The family later regained influence among the Syrian Bedouin; Fadl ibn Rabi'a switched between Crusaders, Seljuks and Fatimids in the early 12th century, and his descendants led the Al Fadl tribe in Mamluk times.

jabal-druze-state.t: A French-created autonomous state for the Druze of the Hawran mountains, where the Great Syrian Revolt of 1925 began.
jabal-druze-state.o: In 1921 France reached an agreement with Druze leaders granting the mountainous Jabal al-Druze, south of Damascus, autonomy under French protection. Salim al-Atrash, of the leading Druze family, became its first governor.
jabal-druze-state.r: The state kept Druze customary leadership, with French advisers. After Salim's death in 1923, the French officer Gabriel Carbillet governed it, imposing roads and land reforms with forced labour and challenging the power of the Atrash chiefs. Druze anger led Sultan al-Atrash to rise in July 1925, defeating French columns and sparking the Great Syrian Revolt, which spread to Damascus before it was crushed in 1927.
jabal-druze-state.e: The state was renamed Jabal al-Arab, and under the 1936 Franco-Syrian treaty it was joined to the Syrian Republic, becoming the province of Suwayda.

jasrota-state.t: A minor Rajput hill state near Kathua, one of the small principalities absorbed by the Dogra rulers of Jammu in the early 19th century.
jasrota-state.o: Jasrota was ruled by the Jasrotia Rajputs, a branch related to the ruling family of Jammu. Tradition dates the state to around 1400, but its early history is poorly recorded.
jasrota-state.r: A small state between the Ravi and the Ujh in the lower hills, Jasrota was overshadowed by its neighbours Jammu and Basohli. Little is known of its internal history.
jasrota-state.e: In the early 19th century Jasrota was absorbed by the Dogras under the Sikh Empire, and it became part of Jammu and Kashmir (princely state) in 1846. The area is now in Kathua district.

jalia-devani-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Kathiawar peninsula, one of the many small estates of the Halar country.
jalia-devani-state.o: Jalia Devani was a small estate in Kathiawar, held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its origins are known mainly from local tradition and colonial lists.
jalia-devani-state.r: The ruler held a handful of villages and, after 1807, came under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency. Few further details are recorded.
jalia-devani-state.e: Jalia Devani merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960.

judicate-of-logudoro.t: The northern Sardinian kingdom of Torres, one of four native judicates that ruled the island after Byzantine authority faded and a patron of Sardinia's finest Romanesque churches.
judicate-of-logudoro.o: As Byzantine control over Sardinia lapsed in the 10th and early 11th centuries, the island divided into four self-governing realms ruled by judges (judikes). Logudoro, also called Torres after the old Roman port of Porto Torres, covered the north-west. Its rulers held court at Ardara and appear in documents from the early 11th century.
judicate-of-logudoro.r: The judge ruled with an assembly of notables, the corona de logu, and governed through curatorie, rural districts. Land registers called condaghes were kept in Sardinian, among the earliest texts in the language. Judges invited Benedictine, Camaldolese and Vallombrosan monks, who built churches such as the Santissima Trinità di Saccargia, while Pisa and Genoa competed for its trade and favour.
judicate-of-logudoro.e: The last ruler, Adelasia, married Enzo, son of Emperor Frederick II, but died without heirs in 1259. The realm was then carved up between the Doria and Malaspina families, the Judicate of Arborea and the town of Sassari, which became the Republic of Sassari.

jimara-kaabu.t: One of the three royal provinces of the Kaabu Empire, stretching from Guinea-Bissau toward the Gambia river.
jimara-kaabu.o: Jimara was a province of the Mandinka Kaabu Empire, which emerged from the westward expansion of the Mali Empire and became independent in the 16th century. It lay in the north-east of Kaabu, near the Gambia river. Its history is known mainly from oral tradition.
jimara-kaabu.r: With Sama and Pachana, Jimara was one of the provinces whose Nyancho warrior nobility, reckoned through the female line, supplied the Mansaba of Kaabu in rotation. Its own mansa ruled with local lineage heads, and its economy rested on farming, slave raiding and trade with river ports.
jimara-kaabu.e: Jimara was weakened by Fulani rebellions and attacks from the Imamate of Futa Jallon in the 19th century. After Kaabu's fall in 1867 its lands were absorbed into Fuladu and later divided between Portuguese Guinea and the British Gambia.

javad-khanate.t: A small lowland khanate at the meeting of the Kura and Araxes rivers in central Azerbaijan, one of the least documented of the Caucasian khanates.
javad-khanate.o: After the death of Nader Shah in 1747, the governors of the district around the town of Javad, at the confluence of the Kura and Araxes, made themselves hereditary khans. The khanate covered the lowland steppe of Mughan and the river crossings that linked Shirvan, Karabakh and Persia.
javad-khanate.r: Its people lived from irrigated farming, livestock and fishing in the great rivers, and the crossings at Javad were an important route. Too weak to stand alone, the khanate was dominated by stronger neighbours, and from 1768 to 1789 it was a dependency of Fatali Khan of the Quba Khanate.
javad-khanate.e: As Russia advanced into the eastern Caucasus, the khanate submitted, and around 1805 the Russian Empire absorbed it. The town of Javad declined, and its lands were divided among neighbouring districts.

jaso-state.t: A small Bundela principality of the Bundelkhand Agency, one of several minor holdings created from the lands of Chhatrasal's descendants.
jaso-state.o: Jaso was founded in the 18th century by a branch of the Bundela Rajputs who descended from Chhatrasal of Panna. Its chief received a British sanad in the early 19th century.
jaso-state.r: Little is recorded about the state beyond its listing as a minor, non-salute state of the Bundelkhand Agency covering a small group of villages.
jaso-state.e: After independence Jaso was merged into Vindhya Pradesh with the other Bundelkhand states, and its former territory lies in Satna district of Madhya Pradesh.

jubbal-state.t: A Rajput hill state in the upper Pabbar valley east of Shimla, one of the larger Simla Hill States and a source of fine deodar timber.
jubbal-state.o: Tradition holds that the ruling family was founded around 1200 by a branch of the Sirmur royal house. For much of its history Jubbal was a tributary of Sirmur State.
jubbal-state.r: Jubbal was a mountain state of forests and terraced fields, whose deodar timber was a valuable resource in the British period. Gurkhas of the Kingdom of Nepal occupied it in the early 19th century. After the Anglo-Nepalese War the British took over its affairs and later restored the Rana as an independent Simla Hill State. Little else is recorded of its history.
jubbal-state.e: Jubbal merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now in Shimla district.

jaffna-kingdom.t: The Tamil kingdom of northern Sri Lanka ruled by the Aryacakravarti dynasty from Nallur until the Portuguese conquest in 1619.
jaffna-kingdom.o: A kingdom in the Jaffna peninsula emerged after Kalinga Magha's invasion of Polonnaruwa around 1215. By the late 13th century it was held by the Aryacakravarti dynasty, which originated as Pandya commanders from the Rameswaram area and established itself at Nallur under the overlordship of the Later Pandyan Empire.
jaffna-kingdom.r: At its height in the 14th century the kingdom controlled the pearl fisheries of the Gulf of Mannar and collected tribute from the Vanni chieftaincies and parts of the Sinhalese west coast. Ibn Battuta visited its king in 1344. The court supported Hindu temples, including Nallur Kandaswamy, and Tamil literature on astrology and medicine.
jaffna-kingdom.e: The Kingdom of Kotte occupied Jaffna from about 1450 to 1467. In the 16th century the Portuguese intervened repeatedly, and after Cankili II's resistance they annexed the kingdom in 1619, adding it to Portuguese Ceylon. Jaffna remains the cultural heart of Sri Lankan Tamil society.

jingnan.t: The smallest of the Ten Kingdoms, a cluster of prefectures around Jiangling on the Yangtze that survived for four decades by bowing to every larger neighbour.
jingnan.o: Gao Jixing, a former slave adopted into a household close to Zhu Wen, was appointed military governor of Jingnan at Jiangling by the Later Liang in 907. After the Later Tang took power he was made Prince of Nanping in 924, and his family ruled the region as hereditary lords.
jingnan.r: With only three prefectures, Jingnan lived by diplomacy and commerce. It sat at a crossroads of Yangtze river trade, and its rulers accepted titles from the northern dynasties and from southern states such as Wu (Ten Kingdoms) and Later Shu at the same time. Other courts mocked them as 'Gao the Shameless' for seizing passing tribute and then apologising, but the policy kept the state alive.
jingnan.e: In 963 Song Dynasty troops, sent through Jingnan on a campaign in Hunan, occupied Jiangling, and Gao Jichong surrendered without fighting. His family was treated generously, and Jingnan's fall was the first step in the Song conquest of the southern kingdoms.

jin-five-dynasties.t: The Shatuo Turkic principality of Li Keyong and Li Cunxu at Taiyuan, the Later Liang's great rival, which conquered it and became the Later Tang.
jin-five-dynasties.o: Li Keyong, chief of the Shatuo Turks, helped the Tang drive Huang Chao out of Chang'an in 883 and was rewarded with the governorship of Hedong, centred on Taiyuan. He was made Prince of Jin in 895. When Zhu Wen ended the Tang and founded the Later Liang in 907, Li Keyong refused to submit.
jin-five-dynasties.r: Jin was a military state built on Shatuo and other cavalry. It continued to use the Tang reign title as a sign of loyalty to the old dynasty. Li Keyong's son Li Cunxu, succeeding in 908, defeated the Liang at Bochao in 911, annexed the Yan (Five Dynasties) of Liu Shouguang in 913 and won most of Hebei.
jin-five-dynasties.e: In 923 Li Cunxu proclaimed himself emperor of a restored Tang at Daming and within months captured Kaifeng, ending the Later Liang. Jin thus became the Later Tang, and the Shatuo Turks went on to found three of the Five Dynasties.

jamaica.t: The largest English-speaking island of the Caribbean, independent since 1962 and a parliamentary monarchy famed worldwide for reggae and athletics.
jamaica.o: After Jamaicans voted to leave the West Indies Federation in 1961, the Colony of Jamaica became independent on 6 August 1962 as a Commonwealth realm, with the British monarch as head of state and Alexander Bustamante of the Jamaica Labour Party as prime minister.
jamaica.r: Politics has been a contest between the Jamaica Labour Party and the People's National Party. Michael Manley's democratic socialist government of 1972 to 1980 raised the bauxite levy and allied with Cuba, while political violence culminated in about 800 deaths around the 1980 election, won by Edward Seaga. Bauxite, tourism, remittances and agriculture are the main economic pillars. Rastafari and reggae, led by Bob Marley, made Jamaican culture globally influential.
jamaica.e: Jamaica remains a parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy, although governments have pledged to become a republic. It has faced high debt and violent crime, while its athletes, such as Usain Bolt, have dominated world sprinting.

jath-state.t: A small Maratha state of the Deccan, ruled by the Daphle family of Chavan Deshmukhs on the dry eastern edge of Satara.
jath-state.o: Jath was founded in 1686 when the Chavan family, later known as Daphle, received the deshmukhi of the Jath area from the Adil Shahi sultans of Bijapur. They retained it under the Marathas.
jath-state.r: The Daphles ruled a dry, drought-prone territory of millet and sheep farming. After 1818 the state came under British protection and was grouped among the Southern Maratha Jagirs, later under the Deccan States Agency. Few further details of its rulers are widely recorded.
jath-state.e: Jath merged into Bombay Province in 1948 and became part of Maharashtra in 1960. It now lies in Sangli district.

japanese-occupation-of-the-dutch-east-in.t: Japanese military rule of the Indonesian archipelago from 1942 to 1945, which ended Dutch power and opened the way to independence.
japanese-occupation-of-the-dutch-east-in.o: Seeking oil and raw materials, Japan invaded the Dutch East Indies from January 1942. After the Battle of the Java Sea, the Dutch forces surrendered at Kalijati on 8 March 1942. The colony was divided between the Japanese 16th Army on Java, the 25th Army on Sumatra and the navy in the eastern islands.
japanese-occupation-of-the-dutch-east-in.r: The Japanese interned Dutch civilians, banned the Dutch language and renamed Batavia Jakarta. They co-opted nationalist leaders such as Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta, created mass organisations and the PETA volunteer army, but also requisitioned rice and conscripted hundreds of thousands of romusha labourers, causing famine and great loss of life.
japanese-occupation-of-the-dutch-east-in.e: As defeat neared, Japan allowed a committee to prepare independence, and Sukarno set out the Pancasila principles in June 1945. Two days after Japan surrendered, Sukarno and Hatta proclaimed the independence of Indonesia on 17 August 1945.

johor-sultanate.t: The successor of the Malacca Sultanate, once ruling Johor, Riau and Singapore, and still a monarchy within Malaysia today.
johor-sultanate.o: After the Portuguese took Malacca in 1511, Sultan Mahmud Shah's son Alauddin Riayat Shah II founded a new court on the Johor River around 1528. Johor Lama became the capital of a state claiming Malacca's heritage over the southern peninsula and the Riau islands.
johor-sultanate.r: Johor fought a long triangular war with Portuguese Malacca and the Aceh Sultanate, then allied with the Dutch to take Malacca in 1641. The murder of Sultan Mahmud Shah II in 1699 ended the Malacca line, and the bendahara's family took the throne. In the 18th century Bugis nobles held real power in Riau.
johor-sultanate.e: In 1819 the British recognised Hussein Shah as sultan to secure Singapore, and the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 split the realm, leaving Riau-Lingga to the Dutch. The temenggung's line, led by Abu Bakar, built modern Johor Bahru. Johor joined Malaya, and Sultan Ibrahim became King of Malaysia in 2024.

jind-state.t: One of the three Phulkian Sikh states of Punjab, linked by marriage to the Sikh Empire of Ranjit Singh.
jind-state.o: Gajpat Singh, a descendant of Phul, seized the area of Jind around 1763 after the fall of Mughal Sirhind, and received the title of Raja from the Mughal emperor in 1772. His daughter Raj Kaur married Maha Singh of Sukerchakia and was the mother of Ranjit Singh.
jind-state.r: Jind accepted British protection in 1809. Its capital moved to Sangrur, and Raja Sarup Singh's support for the British in 1857 earned him new lands. Jind had a 13-gun salute and a mixed Sikh and Hindu Jat population. Ranbir Singh ruled from 1887 until 1948.
jind-state.e: Jind acceded to India in 1947 and in 1948 was merged into the Patiala and East Punjab States Union. Its lands are now divided between Punjab and Haryana.

jaipur-state.t: The Kachhwaha Rajput kingdom of Amber and Jaipur, a close partner of the Mughal emperors whose 18th-century ruler built the planned city of Jaipur and its observatory.
jaipur-state.o: The Kachhwaha Rajputs established themselves in the Dhundhar region of eastern Rajasthan in the 11th and 12th centuries; tradition credits Dulha Rai with the founding, and Amber became their capital. Their rise began when Raja Bharmal allied with Akbar in 1562 and gave him his daughter in marriage.
jaipur-state.r: Kachhwaha princes became leading Mughal nobles: Man Singh I was one of Akbar's chief generals and governors. Sawai Jai Singh II founded Jaipur in 1727 on a grid plan and built astronomical observatories, the Jantar Mantar, at Jaipur, Delhi and other cities. The state prospered from banking, gem cutting and trade.
jaipur-state.e: Jaipur signed a treaty with the British in 1818. In 1949 Maharaja Man Singh II merged it into Greater Rajasthan, with Jaipur as the capital, and he became Rajpramukh. The city remains Rajasthan's capital.

junior-juz.t: The western division of the Kazakhs, whose khan Abulkhair first accepted Russian protection in 1731.
junior-juz.o: After Tauke Khan's death around 1718, the Kazakh Khanate split, with the Junior Juz holding the western steppe between the Aral Sea, the Caspian and the Ural River. Its tribes belonged to the Alimuly, Baiuly and Zhetiru groupings.
junior-juz.r: Under pressure from the Dzungars and the Kalmyk Khanate, Abulkhair Khan sought Russian protection, which was formalised in 1731. Russia built Orenburg in 1743 as a trading and military base on its border. The juz was nomadic, raiding and trading with Russia and Khiva. Syrym Datuly led a long revolt against both the khans and Russia from 1783.
junior-juz.e: Part of the Junior Juz formed the Bukey Horde in 1801. Russia abolished the khanship of the Junior Juz in 1824 and divided it into administrative districts, a process completed after the revolt of Isatay Taimanuly in the 1830s.

jalayirids.t: A Mongol dynasty that ruled Iraq and Azerbaijan after the Ilkhanate, whose court at Baghdad and Tabriz fostered a golden age of Persian painting.
jalayirids.o: The Jalayirs were a Mongol tribe prominent in the Ilkhanate. After the Ilkhan Abu Sa'id died in 1335 without an heir, Hasan Buzurg ('Hasan the Tall') set up puppet khans and by 1336 to 1340 controlled Baghdad and Iraq, fighting the Chupanids for Azerbaijan.
jalayirids.r: Hasan's son Shaykh Uways (1356 to 1374) took Tabriz in 1360 and ruled both Iraq and Azerbaijan. The Jalayirids presented themselves as heirs of the Ilkhans and patronised Persian culture: the poet Salman Savaji praised them, and Jalayirid manuscript painters, such as Junayd, shaped the later Timurid style. Ahmad Jalayir, a poet and calligrapher himself, held Baghdad against repeated attacks.
jalayirids.e: Timur drove Ahmad from Baghdad in 1393 and 1401. Ahmad returned but was killed by Qara Yusuf of the Qara Qoyunlu in 1410. Jalayirid remnants held parts of southern Iraq until 1432.

jarvamaa.t: Inland county at the heart of Estonia, conquered in the early 13th century and later a key holding of the Livonian Order.
jarvamaa.o: Järvamaa, Jerwia in Latin, occupied the central plateau of Estonia, bordering most of the other Estonian lands. Its central position made it a crossroads, and it appears often in Henry of Livonia's chronicle of the crusade.
jarvamaa.r: Järvamaa's elders joined the alliances of the Estonian counties against the crusaders and their Latvian allies. Its people farmed the limestone plateau and maintained hillforts as places of refuge. Its leaders accepted baptism after repeated raids around 1220.
jarvamaa.e: Fought over by Danes and the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, Järvamaa was assigned to the Livonian Order by the Treaty of Stensby in 1238. The Order built Weissenstein (Paide) castle there in 1265, and the region remained Order territory until the Livonian War.

jaitpur-state.t: A Bundela state of Bundelkhand formed from Chhatrasal's kingdom and annexed by the British under the doctrine of lapse in 1849.
jaitpur-state.o: When Maharaja Chhatrasal died in 1731, his realm was divided between his sons and the Peshwa. Jagat Raj received the eastern share centred on Jaitpur, while his brother Hirde Sah held Panna.
jaitpur-state.r: The Jaitpur line held its lands through the Maratha period and accepted British supremacy after 1803. Its Raja Parichhat was deposed in 1842 for backing the Bundela rising, and a relative was installed in his place. Little else is recorded of the state's administration.
jaitpur-state.e: When the installed ruler died without a natural heir in 1849, Lord Dalhousie annexed Jaitpur under the doctrine of lapse, one of the first states taken that way. Its lands, around Jaitpur in today's Mahoba district of Uttar Pradesh, became British territory.
